title: Major Health Systems Deploying and Expanding Oracle Health EHR
script:
Alex: Good morning, Sam. We're looking at a market today that feels like it’s pulling in two completely opposite directions.

Sam: It really is, Alex. On one hand, we’re seeing half a trillion dollars of underlying digital infrastructure being built out. On the other, one of the biggest payors is bracing for a significant financial hit, directly impacting millions of lives.

Alex: Exactly. The digital transformation keeps accelerating, but the fundamentals of how we pay for care are still subject to some very old, very painful realities.

Sam: Welcome to Healthcare Daily Pulse, this Monday, October 12th.

---

Alex: Kicking us off today, we have some significant news from the provider side.

Sam: Major Health Systems Deploying and Expanding Oracle Health EHR.

Alex: So, we're talking about Billings Clinic-Logan Health, a 30-hospital system, committing to a three-year Oracle Health rollout. Huntsville Hospital Health System standardizing on Oracle, and Baystate Health expanding their existing collaboration.

Sam: From a health system CEO's perspective, this isn't just about software; it's about foundational strategy. These are massive capital investments that dictate how care is delivered for the next decade. The real question is how they future-proof their operations, improve patient safety, and drive better outcomes through better data.

Alex: "Future-proof" is a nice aspiration, Sam. But from where I sit, these are multi-hundred-million-dollar commitments with notoriously long implementation cycles and even longer ROI horizons. Medical loss ratio is the whole story here for the payors covering these systems. For the systems themselves, the capital outlay is staggering. How exactly does this bend the cost curve? Because pilots don't bend curves, and I’m not seeing a clear path to reduced spending or even significantly improved efficiency that offsets the investment.

Sam: But Alex, a CEO isn't just looking at the immediate cost curve. They're looking at the strategic necessity. Interoperability is a huge driver here. Consolidating onto a single platform like Oracle Health means breaking down data silos, which is critical for population health management, for clinical decision support, and frankly, for attracting and retaining top clinicians who expect modern tools. Workforce eats strategy, and if your EHR is clunky, you lose talent.

Alex: So, the argument is that better tools retain staff, which somehow offsets the cost of the tools themselves? I need to see the unit economics on that, Sam. What's the actual dollar-for-dollar return on that interoperability? Because these systems are still going to be dealing with claims processing, denials, and all the administrative friction that an EHR, no matter how shiny, doesn't magically solve. This feels more like keeping up with the Joneses than a disruptive strategy.

Sam: It's not about magic, it's about foundation. A modern EHR *can* reduce administrative burden over time through better automation and integration. It *can* improve patient flow and reduce errors, which impacts length of stay and readmissions – clear cost drivers. For a CEO, not investing means falling behind, losing market share, and being unable to participate in value-based care models effectively because your data infrastructure isn't there. Patients feel this before spreadsheets do; a fragmented system means a fragmented patient experience.

Alex: I'll concede that a fragmented system is a problem. But the track record of EHR implementations delivering on these grand promises of efficiency and cost reduction... it’s spotty at best. Many of these are just incredibly expensive operational necessities that rarely live up to the hype in terms of actual cost savings. It's a massive investment just to stay in the game, not necessarily to transform it. We’re talking about moving from one set of challenges to another, often with a bigger bill.

Sam: But the alternative for these large systems isn't viable. You can't run a 30-hospital system on disparate, aging software. The strategic decision for these CEOs isn't "if" they upgrade, but "with whom." Oracle Health, post-Cerner acquisition, is clearly making inroads by leveraging its broader tech stack. It's a long game, Alex, but one they can't afford to lose. The ability to collect and analyze data across an entire system opens up possibilities for genuine care model innovation that simply aren't possible otherwise.

Alex: Data collection is one thing. Meaningful analytics that change behavior and improve outcomes at a population level? That’s another beast entirely. It’s a slide, not a strategy, until I see the actual proof points on the cost side.

---

[TRANSITION]

---

Sam: Speaking of technology and data, our next story gives us a glimpse into the sheer scale of the digital infrastructure underpinning so much of what we discuss in healthcare.

Alex: Amazon Web Services Reports $496 Billion Backlog and 37% Revenue Growth.

Sam: That's a staggering number, Alex. Almost half a trillion dollars in committed future revenue and a third growth year over year. From the perspective of a digital health operator, this isn't just a tech story; it’s a direct indicator of the robust demand for the scalable, secure cloud computing infrastructure that powers everything from telehealth platforms to AI-driven diagnostics, electronic health records.

Alex: It's certainly a massive number. But from a payor analyst perspective, my first thought is, how much of that growth translates into tangible cost savings or improved health outcomes *within healthcare*? AWS is the plumbing. It's necessary, yes, but the cost of the plumbing doesn't tell me if the water flowing through it is clean or if it's being used efficiently. This signifies capacity, not necessarily value realization for our sector.

Sam: But Alex, you can't have value realization without the capacity. This growth signals that the underlying infrastructure is robust enough to handle the immense data loads and processing power required for advanced analytics, machine learning, and AI in healthcare. For a digital health operator, this means less worry about scaling infrastructure and more focus on building innovative solutions. The cost of running these sophisticated platforms is coming down, or at least becoming more predictable, because of providers like AWS. This enables smaller startups and even large systems to experiment and deploy faster.

Alex: I agree it enables, Sam. But enabling isn't solving. We've seen countless digital health "innovations" built on robust cloud infrastructure that failed to bend the cost curve or meaningfully impact health. Follow the risk adjustment, and you’ll see how many of these pilots never scale. This AWS growth is a proxy for *investment capacity*, not necessarily for *validated healthcare impact*. It's critical, absolutely, but it’s a means to an end, not the end itself.

Sam: It's the engine, Alex. You can't drive anywhere without it. The real question is how healthcare leaders leverage this engine. We're talking about the backbone for remote patient monitoring, for predictive analytics that can prevent hospitalizations, for personalized medicine. All of that relies on massive computing power and secure data storage. The fact that AWS has this kind of demand and growth means the industry as a whole is committing deeply to a digital future. That commitment then allows digital health operators to innovate without constantly rebuilding the wheel.

Alex: I'll grant you it's the engine, Sam. But healthcare is still driving a very old car, and just putting a new engine in it doesn't solve the fundamental design flaws. We still have immense interoperability challenges *between* systems, regulatory hurdles, and adoption issues at the provider level. A half-trillion-dollar backlog for AWS is great for Amazon, but it's a proxy for the *potential* for digital transformation, not necessarily its *successful execution* in healthcare specifically. It’s a foundational piece, but it’s a piece that often gets more attention than the actual outcomes it enables.

Sam: It speaks to confidence, though. The market is pouring money into the belief that digital transformation *will* eventually pay off. Digital health operators see this as the permission structure to build bigger, faster, and more securely. It's a huge tailwind.

Alex: A tailwind that still needs a very specific, measured strategy to convert into actual value for the patient and the payor. Otherwise, it’s just more compute power for more expensive, ineffective solutions.

---

[TRANSITION]

---

Sam: Now, from the foundational tech driving future innovation, let's pivot sharply to the present financial realities for one of the largest government-sponsored health plan operators.

Alex: Centene Corporation Sees Institutional Investment Boost and Provides Q3 Outlook.

Sam: The headline sounds positive with the institutional investment boost, but the facts tell a different story. Centene's Q3 2026 adjusted EPS is expected to be around $0.25, a massive drop from Q2's $2.51. And they're forecasting Medicaid membership to decline 8-9% in 2026, worsening from a prior 6% forecast.

Alex: This is my world, Sam, and the numbers here are very concerning for any payor analyst. The institutional investment, while notable, is almost a distraction from the core financial health indicated by that EPS guidance. A projected 90% drop in adjusted EPS quarter-over-quarter is a flashing red light. Medical loss ratio is the whole story here, and the Medicaid redeterminations are hitting them hard. An 8-9% decline in Medicaid membership for a company like Centene is a significant P&L event.

Sam: It's a significant human event, too, Alex. That decline in Medicaid membership isn't just a number on a spreadsheet; it represents millions of individuals losing their health coverage. From an operational perspective, this is a nightmare for a health plan. They have to manage the churn, the outreach, the potential for members to cycle back on and off coverage. Patients feel this before spreadsheets do. It's disruptive to care continuity and creates enormous administrative burden for states and plans alike.

Alex: Absolutely, the human cost is real, and the operational challenges are immense. But from a financial perspective, this is about revenue contraction and the costs associated with it. Centene's business model is heavily reliant on government programs. A steeper decline in Medicaid enrollment means less premium revenue, and while some costs might go down, the fixed costs of administering the plan don't necessarily scale linearly. The fact that their forecast worsened from 6% to 8-9% indicates an accelerating trend they're struggling to contain. It suggests ongoing instability in that market segment.

Sam: And it underscores how intertwined health plan strategy is with government policy. The unwinding of the public health emergency provisions around Medicaid has created this massive wave of redeterminations. For Centene, it means they have to pivot their strategy, perhaps focusing more on other lines of business or tightening their belt significantly. Workforce eats strategy here too; you have to adjust your staffing and operations to a smaller member base, which is incredibly difficult to do efficiently.

Alex: It's not just policy; it's execution. Other plans are navigating this too. This sharper decline suggests Centene might be experiencing a disproportionate impact or facing unique challenges in retaining members or transitioning them to other plans. The increased stake from Farther Finance Advisors is interesting, but it could be a value play on a depressed stock rather than a vote of confidence in immediate recovery. I'd be looking closely at their administrative expense ratio and how they manage the medical expense ratio with a shrinking, potentially sicker, population. Follow the risk adjustment here; those who are left on Medicaid might have higher acuity.

Sam: It's a tough environment, no doubt. It also highlights the vulnerability of payors heavily concentrated in one segment. Diversification becomes key. But the sheer scale of people losing coverage is a systemic issue, not just a Centene problem.

Alex: It's a systemic issue, but Centene's specific numbers give us a window into the financial stress it places on the operators in that system. This is what a significant market shift looks like on the P&L.

---

Alex: So, today we've seen the healthcare industry making massive, foundational investments in technology, hoping to build a better future.

Sam: While simultaneously grappling with the very real, immediate financial pressures and human impacts of policy shifts in the present.

Alex: It's a constant tension between the ambitious long game and the urgent realities of the balance sheet.

Sam: Thanks for joining us on Healthcare Daily Pulse. We’ll be back tomorrow to continue charting these complex currents.

title: Employers Anticipate 8.2% Increase in Health Benefit Costs for 2027, Highest Since 2003
script:
Alex: How many more percentage points of premium can we realistically shift to employees before we break the system, not just their budgets?

Sam: Good morning, and welcome to Healthcare Daily Pulse, your essential Monday morning briefing for October 12th. I'm Sam.

Alex: And I'm Alex. That question, Sam, is what every employer benefits leader is wrestling with today. Let's dive into it.

Sam: Absolutely. Our first story hits directly on that point, and it's a tough one.

Alex: **Employers Anticipate 8.2% Increase in Health Benefit Costs for 2027, Highest Since 2003**

Sam: This Marsh report is stark, Alex. Employers are bracing for an 8.2% rise in health benefit costs for 2027, even after they implement planned cost-reduction measures. Without those measures, we're looking at an 11% hike.

Alex: The medical loss ratio is the whole story here, isn't it? An 8.2% increase, after *planned* cost reductions, tells you how much pressure is building. It’s a direct hit to the bottom line for every company, large or small. For a CFO, this isn't just a benefits line item; it's a significant drag on earnings per share.

Sam: It is, and the human cost is substantial too. Approximately two-thirds of large employers expect workers to absorb a greater share of premium costs in 2027. We already know from KFF that workers at smaller firms are paying significantly more for family coverage. This isn't just numbers on a spreadsheet for employees; it's less take-home pay, less disposable income, and for some, a real choice between health coverage and other necessities.

Alex: That's the part that always gets overlooked in these projections. When you push more cost onto employees, you're not actually bending the cost curve. You're just shifting it. And what happens when you shift it too far? You get adverse selection. Healthier employees opt out, leaving a sicker pool, driving per-member costs even higher. It’s a death spiral in slow motion.

Sam: I agree that merely shifting costs isn isn't a long-term solution. It's a stopgap. But the real question is, what can employers *do*? They're caught between a rock and a hard place. They want to provide good benefits to attract and retain talent, but these increases are unsustainable. Workforce eats strategy, and if your benefits are eroding, your workforce is going to feel it. This impacts morale, productivity, and ultimately, a company’s ability to compete.

Alex: They can do what works. Follow the risk adjustment. Invest in care models that truly reduce utilization of high-cost services. But what I see, Sam, are more pilot programs, more promises of "innovative solutions" that never scale. An 8.2% increase *after* planned cost reductions tells me those planned reductions aren't hitting hard enough, or they're just delaying the inevitable. What are these employers *actually* planning to do? More narrow networks? Higher deductibles? Those are blunt instruments.

Sam: They are, and often counterproductive for patients who then delay care, leading to more expensive interventions down the line. But I've been in those strategy meetings, Alex. It's incredibly complex. They're looking at everything from direct contracting to advanced primary care models, but implementing those takes time, capital, and significant internal change management. It's not just "switch to a new plan." It's about changing how care is accessed and delivered.

Alex: But the math doesn't lie. If the cost curve isn't bending, if the medical loss ratio continues to climb, then the strategies aren't working at scale. Pilots don't bend curves. What’s the unit economics of these "innovative" solutions? Are they actually reducing the per-member per-month cost, or are they just adding another layer of administrative expense?

Sam: That's a fair challenge. The ROI on many of these interventions is hard to demonstrate quickly, and employers are under quarterly pressure. But if they don't invest in these longer-term strategies, what's the alternative? Continue to chip away at employee benefits until they become meaningless? Patients feel this before spreadsheets do. When someone skips a needed MRI because their deductible is too high, that's a failure of the system, not just a financial decision.

Alex: It is. And it ultimately comes back to the payor and provider landscape. Employers are essentially intermediaries here, stuck passing on costs they don't control. Until we address the fundamental drivers of cost – facility fees, drug prices, administrative complexity – these employer increases will just keep coming. It's a slide, not a strategy, to just pass the buck down the line.

Sam: Exactly. And it creates a cascading effect. Lower-wage workers, smaller businesses, they're hit hardest. It's a real threat to the economic stability of many families. This isn't just a benefits challenge; it's a societal one.

Alex: Agreed. It’s a critical challenge, and one that demands more than just cost-shifting tactics.

[TRANSITION]

Sam: Shifting gears, let's look at a story that highlights strategic success in a different part of the healthcare ecosystem.

Alex: **CVS Health's Aetna Division Reports Over 69% of Medicare Advantage Members in 4-Star Plans or Higher for 2027**

Sam: This is a strong showing for Aetna, Alex. More than two-thirds of their Medicare Advantage members are now in plans rated four stars or higher for 2027. This reflects solid performance across clinical quality, preventive care, and member experience. For CVS Health, this is a significant win.

Alex: It’s a clear win for their MA business, no question. From a payor analyst perspective, this translates directly to revenue. Higher Star Ratings mean higher bonus payments from CMS, which directly impact the medical loss ratio in a positive way. It’s not just about member experience; it’s about substantial financial incentives that flow directly to the bottom line. It’s why every MA plan is laser-focused on these metrics.

Sam: And those metrics are incredibly challenging to achieve and maintain. This isn't just about ticking boxes; it involves significant operational rigor, robust care coordination, and proactive member engagement. Think about the effort required on the ground: ensuring members get their preventive screenings, managing chronic conditions effectively, making sure they understand their benefits and have positive interactions. It's an immense undertaking for a plan of Aetna's size.

Alex: Absolutely. It's a testament to execution. And the market is clearly responding. CVS recently exceeded quarterly expectations, reporting $2.58 in adjusted EPS versus a $1.87 consensus, and $106.1 billion in revenue. Wall Street Zen upgraded them to a "strong-buy" rating. The Star Ratings are a key component of that positive financial sentiment. Follow the risk adjustment, and you follow the stars, in this case.

Sam: It's impressive growth and execution. But the "strong-buy" rating, while justified by current performance, has to contend with the ongoing pressures in the MA landscape. The rules are always changing, the competition is fierce, and we can't forget about the 340B pricing issues that continue to loom. That could still impact future earnings, regardless of how well their clinical teams are performing.

Alex: My skepticism lands softly but firmly here, Sam. While the current performance is excellent, the MA market is a tightrope walk. You're right, 340B is a major unresolved risk. Any policy shift there could significantly impact profitability. And the regulatory environment for MA is constantly evolving. What looks like a strong 4-star today might be harder to maintain next year if CMS tightens the screws on quality measures or payment models. It requires constant, relentless operational optimization just to stay even.

Sam: That's where the "workforce eats strategy" comes in again. To maintain these kinds of Star Ratings, you need highly engaged employees, from the call center to the care managers, to the provider network liaisons. It's a continuum of touchpoints that contribute to that member experience score. This isn't just a finance play; it's a massive operational and human capital achievement.

Alex: And it’s why the investment in vertical integration, like CVS's acquisition of Aetna, makes sense from a payor perspective. Controlling more of the care continuum theoretically allows for better management of these metrics, better coordination, and ultimately, better Star Ratings and higher profits. It’s a strategic play to manage the total cost of care and capture those bonus dollars.

Sam: It definitely is. It illustrates how integrated care models, even if they're still in progress, can translate directly into tangible results, both for the members and for the company's financial health. It’s a testament to the idea that better quality can indeed lead to better financial outcomes, when executed well.

Alex: For now. But I'll be watching the unit economics of those integrated services closely. The long game in MA is about sustainable quality and cost control, not just hitting a Star Rating target in a given year.

[TRANSITION]

Sam: Speaking of innovation and better care, our final story today brings us to the exciting world of digital health and diabetes management.

Alex: **Ascensia Diabetes Care Partners with Sava Technologies to Commercialize Wearable Glucose Microsensor in Europe**

Sam: This is genuinely exciting, Alex. Ascensia Diabetes Care, a major player in diabetes tech, is partnering with Sava Technologies to bring a wearable glucose microsensor to Europe. Ascensia has even led Sava's Series B funding round. This isn't just a distribution deal; it's a strategic investment.

Alex: It's an interesting move. Sava's platform tracks subcutaneous molecules and biomarkers in real time, starting with glucose. The goal is CE approval and release within 18 to 24 months for non-adjunctive use, meaning insulin dosing without routine confirmatory tests. From a payor perspective, the real question is what this means for the total cost of care. Is this truly disruptive, or is it just a better mousetrap for a niche?

Sam: I think it's more than a better mousetrap. Think about the patient experience here. For someone living with diabetes, the ability to track glucose in real-time, with a wearable microsensor, and potentially dose insulin without confirmatory finger pricks? That's a massive leap in convenience and quality of life. Patients feel this before spreadsheets do. This could significantly reduce the burden of diabetes management, improve adherence, and ultimately lead to better glycemic control.

Alex: Improved adherence and control are the holy grail, I agree. But pilots don't bend curves. The market is already saturated with CGMs. What makes this different enough to move the needle on cost? What are the unit economics of this microsensor? Is it significantly cheaper to produce, more accurate, or longer-lasting than existing solutions like Dexcom or Abbott's FreeStyle Libre? Because if it's just incremental improvement in convenience, payors will be slow to adopt unless the cost profile is compelling.

Sam: The "non-adjunctive use" is a key differentiator here, Alex. The ability to use it for insulin dosing without confirmatory tests is a significant step forward, reducing the procedural burden. This isn't just comfort; it's clinical utility. And by starting in Europe, they might be able to scale efficiently before tackling the more complex US market. The partnership with Ascensia, with their established distribution channels and expertise, suggests a strong path to commercialization. This isn't some tiny startup struggling for market access.

Alex: Access is one thing, cost-effectiveness is another. What's the cost per sensor? What's the expected lifespan? Will it integrate seamlessly with existing digital health platforms and EMRs? Because if it adds another siloed data stream, that creates administrative burden for providers, which ultimately translates to cost. This has to fit into a broader care model that demonstrably lowers complications and hospitalizations, not just adds another piece of tech.

Sam: It absolutely has to integrate, and that's where Ascensia's experience will be crucial. But imagine the impact on a med-surg floor, or in a primary care setting, if patients are coming in with significantly better-managed diabetes because they have this non-invasive, highly accurate, real-time data. It reduces the need for urgent care visits due to hypo- or hyperglycemia. It allows for more proactive management by their care team. It genuinely makes care delivery better.

Alex: I'm always cautiously optimistic about technology that promises to make care "better." My question is always: better for whom, and at what cost? For the patient, convenience is great. For the payor, I need to see the evidence that this reduces the medical loss ratio. I need to see the data that shows this prevents complications at a lower overall cost than current interventions. That's the bar.

Sam: And that data will come. But the early adoption and strategic investment from Ascensia tell me they believe it can meet that bar. This is the kind of innovation that, if scaled, doesn't just shift costs but truly improves health outcomes and reduces the long-term burden of chronic disease. Workforce eats strategy, and patients feel this before spreadsheets do. This empowers patients and, potentially, frees up clinical time.

Alex: Empowering patients is good. But "potential" doesn't pay claims. I need to see the unit economics and the hard data on cost reduction. Until then, it's a compelling slide, but not yet a proven strategy for bending the cost curve.

Sam: And that's the tension, isn't it? The vision for better care versus the pragmatic reality of cost. We'll be watching this one closely.

Alex: Indeed. From employers grappling with rising costs to payors strategically managing quality metrics, and new tech promising better care, it's clear the healthcare landscape is in constant motion.

Sam: And we'll be here every day, helping you make sense of the pulse of healthcare. Thanks for joining us on Healthcare Daily Pulse.

Alex: We'll see you tomorrow.
